title: 1 Chronicles 4:24–43
context: The Chronicler turns to Simeon, whose sons are listed with some differences in name and form from the lists in Genesis 46:10 and Numbers 26:12–13; the variations are recorded here as they stand, without harmonizing. Simeon is described as smaller than Judah (4:27), and its towns, many of which also appear in Joshua 19:1–9 in somewhat different forms, are said to have been theirs until David’s reign (4:31). The passage then records two later movements in the days of Hezekiah: some Simeonites went to the entrance of Gedor to find pasture and displaced the people there, including the Meunim, and five hundred went to Mount Seir and struck the remnant of the Amalekites. The location of Gedor, the identity of the Meunim, and the relation of this Amalekite remnant to earlier accounts are uncertain, and interpreters propose different identifications. Arminian and Reformed readers treat the unit as shared ground about God’s preservation of a small tribe, the gift of land and pasture, and the Chronicler’s interest in Israel’s tribes holding their inheritance; neither tradition draws a doctrinal contrast from the list.

verses.text: The sons of Simeon: Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, Shaul;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the sons of Simeon here differ in several names and in number from the lists in Genesis 46:10 and Numbers 26:12–13. The Chronicler records his own list without explaining the differences, and the verse begins the account of a tribe whose survival depended on God’s faithfulness rather than its own size.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise observe the variations from Genesis and Numbers and leave them as they stand, since the text offers no explanation. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler includes Simeon among the tribes of Israel, reminding the restored community that God’s covenant embraced all the tribes, including those that had grown small.

verses.text: Shallum his son, Mibsam his son, and Mishma his son.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the line of Shaul traced through Shallum, Mibsam, and Mishma, each described as his son. This short chain of generations shows continuity within a small tribe and reflects the Chronicler’s concern that the families of Simeon be remembered as part of the whole people of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly note the continuity of the line and see in it God’s preservation of Simeon through the generations. Both traditions agree that the chain of names, though brief, carries the conviction that God had not forgotten even the smaller households of Israel and had kept them within his people.

verses.text: The sons of Mishma: Hammuel his son, Zaccur his son, Shimei his son.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the line continues from Mishma to Shimei, who becomes important in the next verse for the size of his family. The steady chain of names shows how the Chronicler moves from lineage to a comment about the tribe’s growth, preparing for an honest assessment of Simeon’s numbers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise follow the line toward Shimei and see the verse as part of the patient record of God’s dealings with Simeon. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler is not merely listing names but tracing the life of a tribe whose history will include both smallness and later expansion into new pasture lands.

verses.text: Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters; but his brothers didn’t have many children, and all their family didn’t multiply like the children of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the honest comment that Shimei had many children while his brothers did not, so that Simeon did not multiply like Judah. The Chronicler does not explain the cause, and readers should not supply one; the verse simply records that some families grew while others remained small within God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly decline to assign a reason the text does not give, while observing that the comparison with Judah fits the larger picture of Simeon living within Judah’s territory. Both traditions agree that a tribe’s size did not determine its place in God’s covenant, and that the Chronicler honors Simeon even while noting its limits.

verses.text: They lived at Beersheba, Moladah, Hazarshual,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers recognize Beersheba, Moladah, and Hazarshual among the towns also listed for Simeon in Joshua 19:2–3, though some names differ slightly in form. The list reminds readers that the land was God’s gift, distributed to the tribes and remembered through particular places that families called home.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the parallel with Joshua 19 and leave the variations in spelling as they stand. Both traditions see the town list as testimony that God’s promise of land reached even the smaller tribes, and that the Chronicler wished his readers to see these places as part of Israel’s inheritance.

verses.text: at Bilhah, at Ezem, at Tolad,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Bilhah, Ezem, and Tolad continue the list, with Bilhah and Tolad appearing in Joshua 19 in somewhat different forms. The verse adds no commentary, but each town represents a place where Simeonite families lived out their covenant life in the land God had given them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly observe the parallel with Joshua 19 and see the list as part of the record of God’s faithful distribution of the land. Both traditions agree that the locations of some of these towns are uncertain, and that the theological point lies in the inheritance itself rather than in precise identification.

verses.text: at Bethuel, at Hormah, at Ziklag,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers recognize Hormah and Ziklag, towns that appear elsewhere in Israel’s story, with Ziklag later associated with David. The list of Simeonite towns shows how the tribe’s settlements were woven into the wider history of Israel and how the places of God’s people carried memories of his dealings with them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the significance of Ziklag in David’s story and see the town list as preparing for the comment that these were Simeon’s cities until David’s reign. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler’s attention to place serves his larger interest in the land as God’s gift to his covenant people.

verses.text: at Beth Marcaboth, Hazar Susim, at Beth Biri, and at Shaaraim. These were their cities until David’s reign.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the remark that these were Simeon’s cities until David’s reign, which suggests a change in the tribe’s situation at that time, though the text does not describe it. Several of the names, such as Beth Biri and Shaaraim, differ from the forms in Joshua 19:5–6, and the Chronicler records his own list without comment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also take the reference to David’s reign as a marker of change that the text leaves unexplained, and they do not speculate about its causes. Both traditions see in the verse the Chronicler’s sense that Israel’s history moved toward David’s kingdom, and that even tribal settlements were shaped by that larger purpose of God.

verses.text: Their villages were Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan, five cities;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the villages Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan are counted as five cities, while Joshua 19:7 lists four with some different names. The Chronicler preserves his own count without harmonizing, and the verse continues the record of the inheritance God gave Simeon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the difference from Joshua 19:7 and leave it as the text presents it. Both traditions agree that these villages formed part of Simeon’s portion within Judah, and that the Chronicler’s record honors the land as a gift faithfully remembered across the generations of Israel.

verses.text: and all their villages that were around the same cities, as far as Baal. These were their settlements, and they kept their genealogy.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the surrounding villages reached as far as Baal, and that the Simeonites kept their genealogy. The remark shows a tribe that valued its identity and records, which fits the Chronicler’s purpose of helping the restored community understand who they were as God’s people.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the keeping of the genealogy as an expression of covenant identity, preserved through many generations. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler presents this record-keeping positively, since remembering one’s place within God’s people was a way of remembering God’s promises to Israel.

verses.text: Meshobab, Jamlech, Joshah the son of Amaziah,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that a new list of names begins here, leading to the princes described in verse 38. Meshobab, Jamlech, and Joshah are otherwise unknown, but the Chronicler records them as leaders of their families, showing that the tribe had recognized heads who would guide its later movements.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note that these leaders are introduced with little detail and see the list as preparing for the account of Simeon’s expansion. Both traditions agree that the names serve to anchor the coming narrative in real families, and that the Chronicler honors those who led the tribe within God’s people.

verses.text: Joel, Jehu the son of Joshibiah, the son of Seraiah, the son of Asiel,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Joel and Jehu are given short lines of descent, linking them to earlier generations. The verse shows the Chronicler’s care in tracing leaders through their fathers, so that the tribe’s later actions are rooted in a known history among the people God had preserved.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the lines of descent as part of the Chronicler’s emphasis on continuity within Israel. Both traditions agree that the names have no recorded deeds of their own here, yet they are remembered as heads of families through whom God sustained the tribe of Simeon across the generations.

verses.text: Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, Benaiah,
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the list of leaders continues with names such as Elioenai, Asaiah, and Benaiah, several of which appear to include an element referring to God. Without pressing the meaning of each name, the verse reflects a people whose families were shaped by faith in Israel’s God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the many names that seem to honor God, while recognizing that a name alone does not reveal a person’s faith. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler records these leaders as part of the tribe’s remembered story, and that their inclusion underscores God’s care for the families of Simeon.

verses.text: and Ziza the son of Shiphi, the son of Allon, the son of Jedaiah, the son of Shimri, the son of Shemaiah—
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Ziza is traced back through several generations to Shemaiah, closing the list before the summary in verse 38. The careful tracing reflects the Chronicler’s concern that leaders be known by their lineage, which mattered for a community rebuilding its life after exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly see the long line of descent as a mark of the Chronicler’s interest in continuity and order within Israel. Both traditions agree that the verse prepares for the statement that these men were princes in their families, and that God’s preservation of such lines was part of his faithfulness to the tribes.

verses.text: these mentioned by name were princes in their families. Their fathers’ houses increased greatly.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that these named men were princes in their families and that their fathers’ houses increased greatly. The verse balances the earlier note that Simeon did not multiply like Judah, showing that some families did grow, and it prepares for the tribe’s search for new pasture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the contrast with verse 27 and see God’s hand in the growth of these households, without claiming that the text explains how. Both traditions agree that the increase leads naturally into the account that follows, in which the need for pasture drives the Simeonites to move beyond their earlier towns.

verses.text: They went to the entrance of Gedor, even to the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the Simeonites went to the entrance of Gedor, to the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks. The location of this Gedor is uncertain, and it may not be the same place as the Gedor named in the Judah lists. The verse presents an ordinary motive, the needs of shepherds, behind the tribe’s movement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly leave the identification of Gedor open and note the practical reason the text gives for the journey. Both traditions agree that the Chronicler presents the search for pasture without moral comment at this point, and that the account reflects the realities of pastoral life in the land.

verses.text: They found rich, good pasture, and the land was wide, and quiet, and peaceful, for those who lived there before were descended from Ham.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that the Simeonites found rich, good pasture in a wide, quiet, and peaceful land, whose earlier inhabitants were descended from Ham. The description echoes the language of a good land, though the Chronicler does not state a divine promise here; the verse simply reports what they found.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the description of the land and the reference to Ham, which recalls the table of nations in Genesis 10. Both traditions agree that the verse should not be read as a new conquest command, and that its interest lies in the Simeonites’ finding a place where their flocks could thrive.

verses.text: These written by name came in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and struck their tents and the Meunim who were found there; and they destroyed them utterly to this day, and lived in their place, because there was pasture there for their flocks.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that this movement is dated to the days of Hezekiah and that the Simeonites struck the tents of those living there and the Meunim, destroying them and settling in their place. The identity of the Meunim is uncertain. The Chronicler reports the action without explicit approval or condemnation, and readers should be careful not to supply a verdict he does not give.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly observe that the text records the displacement without a stated divine command and without evaluation. Both traditions agree that the verse belongs to the Chronicler’s record of how the tribes held and extended their territory, and both recognize the moral weight of such accounts while not reading more into the brief notice than it says.

verses.text: Some of them, even of the sons of Simeon, five hundred men, went to Mount Seir, having for their captains Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers observe that five hundred Simeonites went to Mount Seir under four captains, the sons of Ishi. The verse records a further expansion beyond Simeon’s earlier towns, and the naming of the captains shows the Chronicler’s concern to anchor the event in known leaders of the tribe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the details of the expedition and the leaders named. Both traditions agree that the text does not explain the motive for this movement beyond its link with the preceding account, and that the identification of the region and its inhabitants at this time remains a matter of interpretation.

verses.text: They struck the remnant of the Amalekites who escaped, and have lived there to this day.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the Simeonites struck the remnant of the Amalekites who had escaped and lived there to this day. Many readers connect this with the long conflict between Israel and Amalek in earlier books, though the text does not make the link explicit, and the relation of this remnant to earlier accounts is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers similarly observe the possible connection to Israel’s earlier conflicts with Amalek, while declining to claim more than the verse states. Both traditions agree that the phrase to this day shows the Chronicler drawing on a source that described the settlement as continuing, and that the unit ends with Simeon established in its place.
